title: Show HN: Lask – A task runner with a type system and pinned Docker environments
body:
I implemented a task runner called Lask. Let me introduce it to you.
Lask is a lightweight task runner with a statically typed DSL. It runs by calling Docker from Lask on the host.
Makefiles or shell scripts I wrote often failed to run on my colleagues' machines, and I lost count of how many times I had to debug them.
YAML-based CI/CD pipelines often fail after waiting for a lot of minutes, which make me angry.
When I was looking for a tool to solve this problem, I found Dagger. Dagger seemed to good for me.
Dagger runs pipelines on Docker, so it is highly portable and can use the type system of general-purpose languages.
However, Dagger was too much for me. Dagger does not run on its own, and requires to set up a general-purpose language ecosystem.
I feel like I was using heavy machinery to move a potted plant. I want to call a tool with only a single binary and one file.
So I decided to create Lask. I want to call simple function with simple command. I want to fix the type and environment of the function.
command { "node", "npm", "npx" } on #node:20.20.2-alpine3.23
test() = $ npm test
$ lask run test
I made a tool that can extract errors immediately by type, run the same way on local and CI, and call simply.
You can use Lask with a single binary of the lask command and Docker installed.
Lask has LSP, so you can use completion and syntax highlighting. You can complete not only the lask command, but also the functions that lask calls.
I considered practical use, so it can be called declared commands, such as `lask cmd psql ...` to check data manually, or `lask cmd kubectl get pods`.
However, Lask does not have as many as Dagger's features, cannot use the advanced ecosystem of general-purpose languages.
Also, Lask is not a build system, so it does not optimize builds by detecting differences. Lask is just a tool to call builder tools.
Lask is licensed under MIT, currently at version 0.7.0 before official release. The implementation is in Haskell. It distributes bina…

title: Comment on: Show HN: Glashütte Trash Clock – A 30-minute pendulum clock made from trash
body:
Ah, but then whose time would that be? How do you keep track of what solar time was parallel to 'your' time?
Time is such a fickle thing. Every atom in the universe knows what time it is, but between the effects of gravity, the speed of light and some quantum stuff it is amazing that we can agree on this at any level at all. I spent a lot of time earlier this year getting some ultra stable clocks to run without shelling out 5 digits and it was a very interesting little detour. Eventually I settled on an old atomic clock module from a decommissioned cell tower, not quite 'miniature' but small enough (I've seen some of the newer ones and they are incredible). The thing is precise enough to show the day/night deviation in phase from DCF77 to my home a few hundred km away.

title: Show HN: Azurade, image and video generation with MCP, credits never expire
body:
Hi HN,
I was frustrated with expiring credits, subscriptions and generally BS approach in image&video generation space (which is now universally useful and basically a commodity) so I've built Azurade, a hosted service where you have 35+ models (Veo3.1, Seedance 2.5, Wan 3.0, Nano Banana, GPT Image2.5 etc.) behind one non-expiring, fully agent native balance.
I care about billing, that's why credits are prepaid and never expire, a failed generation is refunded automatically, and you can buy a pack without a subscription. I got tired of monthly credits (or usage) that vanish at the end of the month

I've ran it through oblivious evaluator agent for 8 times to reach good agent ergonomics. After all, if I want to build an agent-native service the users (agent) should evaluate and correct it.
Please feel free to point your agents at it and send me the nitpicks and gotchas they encounter. Humans are also welcome :)
Demo video (1m40s, cute dog included): https://youtu.be/tX29WLffXCk
P.S. the stack is Go and Pocketbase, official GO MCP SDK, and the frontend is statically rendered NextJS. The access token is an API key named after the client, so revoking an agent means deleting that key on your profile page. It also works like REST API with an OpenAPI spec.

title: Comment on: Dust: Pretraining Transformers Without Backpropagation
body:
Even today's LLMs suddenly get power-competitive when you compare by "power per task". Sure, a GPU can draw 1000W under load. But it also works very fast, and doesn't have to spend any time on things like "sleep".
The trick about comparing the two is that different things are expensive to different substrates.
Coordination is cheap for GPGPU and expensive for brain. When you have a fixed number of reusable general purpose computational units, coordinating execution is more natural than not coordinating execution, and the power cost is nil. When your computational units are independent, purpose specific, and fully embedded into the data path, coordinating them can get less natural and, frankly, optional. When wiring is expensive, coordination can become expensive in turn.
Another thing in the same "cheap for GPGPU but expensive for brain" regime is bandwidth. Look no further than optic nerve to see just how hard it is for nerves to push any appreciable amount of data. Another thing is connectivity. For GPGPU, global connectivity is natural - but the brain has to pay in physical wires for all the connectivity it has, and, see "bandwidth": it doesn't have any good wires. Yet another thing is weight reuse: a big part of why humans get "handedness" is that the brain can't just reuse the motion control circuitry for one hand for another nearly identical hand.
And the final thing I can name off the top of my head is memory - but specifically, memory capable of fast R/W. The capacity of human "working memory" is a disgrace, and not because there was no use for more. Humans rapidly lose visual fidelity of representations for objects they aren't directly looking at, and not at all because "being able to check how things looked 2 seconds ago" is useless. Those capabilities were just too expensive for the substrate to afford them easily.
It's why brains, broadly, favor dataflow-like and SSM-like dynamics, with largely fixed asynchronous dataflows and recurrence over updated lo…

title: Comment on: Powerless F1 drivers frustrated by Bahrain F1 software glitch
body:
Regeneration happens directly on the crankshaft via the mgu-k, not the wheels. The mgu is essentially a governor, so you can set it to add or sink (absorb) torque however you like. If you're adding torque, you're draining the battery, and if you're sinking torque, you're charging the battery. Because everything is mechanically connected, sinking torque also wants to brake the car (i.e. regenerative braking).
In terms of power balance, on average, the draw needs to match generation for the system to work. Since this a race, the battery should be flat when you cross the finish line, because you don't want to leave power on the table. When cars are clipping out on the straights, they're trying to claw back some power for the battery so they can deploy it at a more impactful moment in the race. Maybe it's frustrating for viewers, but part of that is that the vehicle has a maximum sustained power, and a maximum total power, and those aren't the same thing.
The mgu-h was cool, but I believe the teams when they say that it was too difficult and too expensive to get right.

title: Tool or service that tracks deprecations and breaking changes per library version, with an API or feed
body:
I need a tool or service that tells me, for a given library and version, whether it has been
deprecated or whether newer releases contain breaking changes, before I upgrade.

Requirements:

Ecosystems: npm and Maven/Gradle (Android) at least; CocoaPods and Swift Package Manager would be a big plus
Reports deprecations (with dates when available) and breaking changes, not only new versions
Machine-readable access: REST API, RSS/Atom feed or downloadable data
Free or open source preferred; a self-hostable tool is fine
Works from a list of dependencies (e.g. an SBOM or package.json), without uploading source code

What I already tried:

Dependabot / Renovate: they open update PRs, but don't say what breaks before upgrading
OSV and deps.dev: great for vulnerabilities and the npm "deprecated" flag, but no breaking changes
GitHub releases.atom: works, but it's free text per repository, not structured
ChangeRadar: covers developer platforms and AI tools, not libraries

Is there anything that covers this, even partially?

The old version was much simpler, faster, and easier to use. Honestly, the more you improve this app, the less usable it becomes.

title: [early engagement] OAK NATIONAL ACADEMY LIMITED: 2026 ATS & HRIS
body:
Oak National Academy is exploring the replacement of BeApplied, its current Applicant Tracking System (ATS), which is expected to become unavailable at the end of March 2027. Oak is also considering whether to procure a linked HR information system (HRIS) at the same time, procure the systems as separate lots, or address its HRIS needs through a later procurement.
The immediate priority is an ATS that can be implemented in time to maintain recruitment services. Oak is undertaking this engagement to understand the market, test its developing requirements, assess realistic implementation times and decide how best to package the ATS and HRIS requirements. No decision has yet been made to include an HRIS in the resulting tender.
Oak invites input from suppliers of ATS products, HRIS products, integrated ATS and HRIS platforms, and suppliers able to deliver either system with a reliable integration to the other. Suppliers do not need to offer both systems to participate.

title: Natural England: Develop and Supply an Interactive online Nature Finance Project Development game
body:
A self-contained nature finance game that allows players to virtually develop nature recovery projects funded using private and blended finance. Using the GFI Investment Readiness Toolkit as a framework the game will start by presenting players with options such as whether they want to play a seller or buyer, followed by various seller or buyer scenarios. 
Once a player has picked a role they will be taken through the process of developing a nature recovery project using private and blended finance from the start through to signing legal documents and the work starting on the ground. They will do this by working through a series of scenarios. They will have to complete every scenario satisfactorily to be able to move onto the next scenario. Reasons for not completing a scenario properly will be given, as will explanations of why they have completed a scenario correctly. Where possible there will be more than one correct way to complete a scenario.
The game will be for Natural England so will focus on the roles that NE staff are likely to play at each stage of a projects development but will also be able to be used by Environment Agency and Forestry Commission staff carrying out nature finance related roles.
